newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain - AWB sees world pacemaker role.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain - AWB sees world pacemaker role.

text.p: Last week the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) got government approval for the new structure it wanted and a new managing director --- and celebrated by launching an animated cartoon of a predatory shark's fin which prowled the seas to musical accompaniment from the movie Jaws.
The fin debuted at an AWB presentation and dinner in the middle of Grains Week '97 and carried a clear warning -- rest of the world beware, Australian wheat was after ever bigger bites.

Australia's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade Tim Fischer officially launched AWB's world-first foray into branded wheat at the "The Great Australian Bite" dinner, which highlighted the board's international prowess through displays by belly dancers, Indian fire-jugglers and a Chinese dragon.

As the AWB celebrated the successful marketing of a record 23 million tonne crop in 1996/97 and laid claim to expected increasing international success through branded wheat, it showed a strong belief it could remain world market pace-setter.

AWB chairman Trevor Flugge said on Thursday the U.S. was so far behind in world markets "it's not funny". He followed this with a statement on Friday that the AWB's new grower-owned and controlled commercial structure, to take effect from July 1 1999, coupled with monopoly single desk selling, put the AWB "so far ahead of our competitors that they'll never catch us".
One of Flugge's few sombre notes was a prediction that if the U.S. and Europe had reasonable-sized crops this year they would be aggressively using subsidies to buy market share.
But Australia's counter was branded wheat and the "marketing discipline" of the AWB export monopoly, which both allowed wheat to be tailored for specific customers, Flugge said.
Perhaps the single most important point of the week was that the AWB clearly has government backing to retain its export monopoly after the official 1999/2000 competition policy review.

Several AWB leaders privately said after Primary Industries Minister John Anderson announced details of the AWB's restructure that the government decision to "enshrine" the single desk in legislation greatly increased the probability it would remain a permanent feature of wheat export sales.

Branded wheat, meanwhile, is aimed at biting chunks from the top end of world traded wheat rather than simply gobbling market share. Australia saw itself retaining about 20 percent of world traded wheat, given crop availability, but saw revenue produced by that share increasing through branded sales, Flugge said.
Outgoing AWB managing director John Lawrenson said recent international sales had already given AWB wheat premiums of A$12.00 to A$30.00 a tonne over various competitors.
Earlier on Wednesday, Lawrenson's successor as AWB managing director, Kellogg Australia's executive chairman Murray Rogers, showed he did not plan to alter AWB's present course.
"If it's not busted, don't fix it," he told Reuters.

The AWB's big week occurred against the background of five days of meetings by Grains Council of Australia (GCA), where delegates grappled with issues such as grower levies, research and development and quality assurance.
The GCA saw Anderson's statements on the new structure for the AWB as too broad and want clarification of working matters such as statutory powers, proxy rights and tax assurances.
In a week when Australia's focus was on grain politics, markets had a volatile time on local tightness of supply, dry weather concerns and world jitters over the European drought.
Australian wheat futures edged ahead in near-term contracts but rose generally by about A$5.00 a tonne in medium-term and more distant contracts.
Brokers saw prices as headed up.
